Walt Whitman. An American poet who lived from 1819 to 1892 and revolutionized modern verse through his embrace of free form, vernacular language, and the democratic voice. His masterwork, Leaves of Grass, constantly revised throughout his lifetime, celebrates America's diversity, human sexuality, and the individual as part of the broader collective.

Leaves of Grass appeared in 1855 and introduced American poetry to free verse, abandoning traditional meter and rhyme to capture the conversational rhythm and cadence of American speech. His poem "Song of Myself" exemplifies his technique—cataloguing diverse American experiences through a democratic vision that presents a speaker who contains contradictions and encompasses multitudes. Throughout his work, Whitman celebrates the body, sexuality, and sensuality explicitly, breaking Victorian taboos and shocking contemporary readers with frank erotic content and celebration of desire.

His life deeply shaped his poetry. He worked as a journalist, as a nurse during the Civil War caring for wounded soldiers, and as a government clerk. These experiences directly informed his poetry's engagement with American life and suffering. His vision of poetry as a democratic art form—addressing all Americans regardless of education or status, not just an elite audience—redefined the poet's social role and literary mission. This is particularly clear in his profound influence on modernism and Beat poets like Allen Ginsberg, who directly addressed him in the poem "A Supermarket in California."

Leaves of Grass was revised repeatedly throughout Whitman's lifetime, growing larger and more ambitious, showing his ongoing meditation on America, democracy, and the self as process. That influence extends to contemporary poets of identity and political engagement, who inherit his profound belief in poetry as an essential tool for social change and democratic representation.
